For \(\alpha \in N\), consider a relation \(R\) on \(N\) given by \(R=\) \(\{(x, y): 3 x+\alpha y\) is a multiple of 7\(\}\). The relation \(R\) is an equivalence relation if and only if:

options: 4 is the remainder when \(\alpha\) is divided by 10
4 is the remainder when \(\alpha\) is divided by 7
questions.explanation:
For \(R\) to be an equivalence relation, it must be reflexive

So for every \(x \in N,(x, x) \in R\)

That means \(3 x+\alpha x=(3+\alpha) x\) must be divisible by 7 for every \(x\)

This is possible only when \(3+\alpha\) is divisible by 7

So \(\alpha=7 k+4\)

Now relation becomes \(3 x+\alpha y=3 x+(7 k+4) y=3 x+4 y+7 k y\)

So \(3 x+4 y\) must be divisible by 7

If \(3 x+4 y\) is divisible by 7, then \(15 x+20 y\) is also divisible by 7

That is \(x+6 y\), i.e. \(x-y\), is divisible by 7

So \(x-y\) is divisible by 7

Hence \(x\) and \(y\) leave same remainder on division by 7

Therefore \(3 y+4 x\) is also divisible by 7, so relation is symmetric

Also if \((x, y) \in R\) and \((y, z) \in R\), then \(x-y\) and \(y-z\) are divisible by 7

So \(x-z\) is divisible by 7

Hence \(3 x+4 z\) is divisible by 7, so relation is transitive

Therefore \(R\) is an equivalence relation iff \(\alpha\) leaves remainder 4 when divided by 7

questions.question:
Let \( f:[0,1] \to \mathbb{R} \) be a twice differentiable function on \( (0,1) \) such that \( f(0)=3 \) and \( f(1)=5 \). If the line \( y=2x+3 \) intersects the graph of \( f \) at only two distinct points in \( (0,1) \), then the least number of points \( x \in (0,1) \) at which \( f''(x)=0 \) is ?

 

[JEE Main 2022, 28 Jul (Shift 1)]
questions.explanation:
Define \(g(x)=f(x)-(2x+3)\).

The zeros of \(g\) are exactly the points where the graph of \(f\) meets the line \(y=2x+3\).

Since \(f(0)=3\), we get \(g(0)=3-3=0\).

Since \(f(1)=5\), we get \(g(1)=5-5=0\).

The line also intersects the graph at exactly two distinct points inside \((0,1)\).

Let their abscissae be \(a\) and \(b\), where \(0<a<b<1\).

Then \(g(0)=g(a)=g(b)=g(1)=0\).

Thus \(g\) has four distinct zeros in the order \(0<a<b<1\).

By Rolle's theorem on \([0,a]\),

there is a point \(c_1\in(0,a)\) such that \(g'(c_1)=0\).

By Rolle's theorem on \([a,b]\),

there is a point \(c_2\in(a,b)\) such that \(g'(c_2)=0\).

By Rolle's theorem on \([b,1]\),

there is a point \(c_3\in(b,1)\) such that \(g'(c_3)=0\).

Therefore, \(g'\) has at least three distinct zeros \(c_1<c_2<c_3\).

Applying Rolle's theorem to \(g'\) on \([c_1,c_2]\),

there is a point where \(g''=0\).

Applying it again on \([c_2,c_3]\),

there is another distinct point where \(g''=0\).

Hence \(g''\) has at least two zeros in \((0,1)\).

Since \(g(x)=f(x)-(2x+3)\), we have \(g''(x)=f''(x)\).

Therefore, \(f''\) has at least two zeros.

This number can be attained by choosing \(g(x)=x(x-a)(x-b)(x-1)\),

because \(g\) then has exactly the required four zeros and \(g''\) is a quadratic.

Rolle's theorem forces both roots of this quadratic to lie in \((0,1)\),

so there are exactly two.

Hence the least number is \(2\),

Also, \(\dfrac{a_n}{a_{n+2}}=\dfrac{a_na_{n+1}}{a_{n+1}a_{n+2}}=\dfrac{2n}{2(n+1)}=\dfrac{n}{n+1}\).

Therefore, \(\dfrac{a_n+1/a_{n+1}}{a_{n+2}}=\dfrac{2n+1}{2(n+1)}\).

Now \(f'(x)=(2x+1)e^x\), so the only critical point is \(x=-\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Since \(f'(x)<0\) for \(x<-\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(f'(x)>0\) for \(x>-\dfrac{1}{2}\), this point gives the minimum.

Thus, \(f_{\min}=f\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=(-2)e^{-1/2}=-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt e}\), so option B is correct.

The tangent at parameter \(t\) is \(ty=x-\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{t^2}{2}\).

\(\because R=(0,1)\) lies on the tangent,

\(t=-\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{t^2}{2}\)

\(t^2-2t-3=0\)

\((t-3)(t+1)=0\)

\(\therefore t=3,-1\)

The points of contact are \((6,3)\) and \((2,-1)\).

Let \(P=(6,3)\) and \(Q=(2,-1)\).

\(\therefore QP\perp QR\)

Thus, \(\triangle PQR\) is right-angled at \(Q\),

and the orthocentre is \(Q=(2,-1)\).

Then the value of \( |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| \) is equal to:

 

[JEE Main 2022, 28 Jul (Shift 1)]
questions.explanation:
The PDF prints the vector \((x\vec a\times y\vec b)\).

This vector is a scalar multiple of \(\vec a\times\vec b\), so it is automatically perpendicular to both \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\).

\(\therefore\) it is automatically perpendicular to every vector of the form \(6y\vec a-18x\vec b\), and the printed condition gives no restriction on \(\vec b\).

\(\therefore |\vec a\times\vec b|\) cannot be uniquely determined from the question as printed.

In the intended JEE question, the first vector is \(x\vec a+y\vec b\).

Using the intended condition, \((x\vec a+y\vec b)\cdot(6y\vec a-18x\vec b)=0\) for every non-zero pair \((x,y)\).

\(6xy|\vec a|^2-18x^2\vec a\cdot\vec b+6y^2\vec a\cdot\vec b-18xy|\vec b|^2=0\)

The coefficients of \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) must be zero.

\(\vec a\cdot\vec b=0\)

The coefficient of \(xy\) must also be zero.

\(6|\vec a|^2-18|\vec b|^2=0\)

\(|\vec b|^2=\dfrac{|\vec a|^2}{3}=\dfrac{81}{3}=27\)

\(|\vec b|=3\sqrt{3}\)

\(\because \vec a\perp\vec b\), we get \(|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|\).

\(|\vec a\times\vec b|=9(3\sqrt{3})=27\sqrt{3}\)

\(\therefore\) the intended correct option is B

Let the operations \( *, \odot \in\{\wedge, \vee\} \). If \( (p * q) \odot(p \odot \sim q) \) is a tautology, then the ordered pair \( (*, \odot) \) is

 

[JEE Main 2022, 28 Jul (Shift 1)]

The four possible ordered pairs of operations are checked.

For \((\ast,\odot)=(\vee,\wedge)\), the expression is \((p\vee q)\wedge(p\wedge\sim q)=p\wedge\sim q\), which is not a tautology.

For \((\ast,\odot)=(\vee,\vee)\), the expression is \((p\vee q)\vee(p\vee\sim q)\).

\(\Rightarrow (p\vee q)\vee(p\vee\sim q)=p\vee(q\vee\sim q)=p\vee T=T\)

For \((\ast,\odot)=(\wedge,\vee)\), the expression is \((p\wedge q)\vee(p\vee\sim q)=p\vee\sim q\), which is false for \(p=F,q=T\).

The correct ordered pair is \((\vee,\vee)\), so the correct option is \(\mathrm{B}\).

And, \(A^2=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & -1 \\ 2 & \alpha\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & -1 \\ 2 & \alpha\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}-1 & -1-\alpha \\ 2+2 \alpha & \alpha^2-2\end{array}\right]\)

\(\therefore\left|\alpha_1-\alpha_2\right|=|1-(-1)|=2\)

Using \(\displaystyle\lim_{u\to0}\dfrac{\log(1+u)}{u}=1\),
